title: Buddhist funerals
hook: chanting, merit made for the dead, the seventh- and forty-ninth-day rites

segments.voice: Yesterday ended the week with taking vows as a lay person, and a line that asked for no hurry: someday, maybe. Did you write down the vow your mind kept returning to? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

Monks in saffron sit in a row beside a coffin in a Thai temple. A white cloth is laid across a thread that runs from the coffin to the monks, and they chant in Pali. In a Japanese home, incense smoke curls up in front of a photograph, and a priest's voice rises and falls through a sutra. In a Tibetan house, a lama reads aloud to someone who has just died, as if the person can still hear. Three very different rooms. But underneath, the same two things are happening: words of the Dhamma are being spoken, and something good is being done on behalf of the one who has gone. This week begins with Buddhist funerals.
screen: `MONKS CHANTING BESIDE A COFFIN.` → `INCENSE BEFORE A PHOTOGRAPH.` → `A LAMA READING TO THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the chant. At Theravada funerals, the monks may chant a verse that goes back to the Buddha's own passing. In the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, as the Buddha dies, the god Sakka speaks it: impermanent, truly, are all conditioned things; they arise and they pass away; having arisen, they cease; their stilling is happiness. A funeral, in other words, opens by saying the plain truth out loud. Now the second thing: merit for the dead. In a short text called the Discourse Outside the Walls, the departed are described standing outside walls, at crossroads, by doorposts, returning to the homes that were once theirs. When their relatives give food and drink to the monks and say, may this be for our relatives, the departed are said to share in the goodness and give thanks. Weeping and grief, the text says, do not help the dead. Giving does. So at a funeral, families offer robes and food to the monks, and dedicate the merit to the one who died. Then the counting of days. In Tibetan tradition, the text often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead speaks of the in-between state after death lasting up to forty-nine days, and the lama's reading guides the person through it. In China and Japan, tradition holds rites every seventh day until the forty-ninth, when the family gathers again. Across all three rooms, the funeral is not only for grief. It is something the living still get to do for the dead.
screen: `ALL CONDITIONED THINGS PASS.` · `THE DEPARTED OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · `MERIT GIVEN IN THEIR NAME.` · then, large: `THE SEVENTH AND FORTY-NINTH DAYS.`

segments.voice: This one may be tender, so go gently, and skip it if today isn't the day. Sit and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person who has died: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, even someone you only knew a little. See their face, or hear their voice. Then think of one good thing you have done or could do: a kindness, a gift, a meal shared. If it feels right to you, let the thought rest there: may some of this goodness reach them. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Buddhist funerals. Chanting the truth of impermanence, giving in the name of the dead, and marking the days that follow. Today's word.
Your line: merit for the dead. Do one small good thing today, a coin, a meal, a held door, and quietly give it in the name of someone you miss. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: At Buddhist funerals monks or priests chant texts on impermanence, and families make offerings to the monastic community and dedicate the merit to the one who died; in East Asia and Tibet, rites are often held at intervals after the death up to the forty-ninth day.

fork.setup: your relative has died. in the Discourse Outside the Walls, what helps them?
options: giving to the monks and dedicating it to them.
fork.reveal: the text says grief doesn't reach the dead. a gift given in their name does, and they share in the goodness.

original.note: Pali: 'impermanent, truly, are conditioned things', the opening of a verse chanted at Theravada funerals.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funeral is just a way to say goodbye.
what it means: in Buddhist rites, the living chant the truth of impermanence and give merit for the dead.
what a scholar hears: Sakka's verse from the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Tirokudda Sutta on dedicating gifts to the departed, and the forty-nine days of the Tibetan in-between state.

notes: Sakka's verse (anicca vata sankhara...) paraphrased from DN 16; confirm wording and that it is chanted at Theravada funerals.
Tirokudda Sutta paraphrased: the departed outside walls, at crossroads, by doorposts, returning to old homes; 'may this be for our relatives'; weeping does not help. Confirm.
The Bardo Thodol's in-between state 'up to forty-nine days' is attributed to the text; confirm. East Asian seventh-day rites up to the forty-ninth framed as 'tradition holds'.
Hook scenes (the thread from coffin to monks with a cloth, the pamsukula offering; incense before a photograph; a lama reading) are illustrative; confirm.
Practice touches grief: offered with an opt-out. Dedication of merit phrased 'if it feels right to you'; not a new prayer, a description of the dedication. Confirm.
Original-language line in Devanagari Pali; confirm spelling and transliteration.
